title: Sleep, Insomnia & the Psychology of Rest
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

glossary.definition: A drive for sleep that generally grows while we stay awake and reduces during sleep.
glossary.example: After a long day awake, someone begins to feel increasingly sleepy.
glossary.limit: A nap can reduce some sleep pressure even if somebody still wants an early night.

glossary.definition: Internal daily rhythms that influence when the body is prepared for sleep and wakefulness.
glossary.example: A night-shift worker finds the morning alerting despite a long period awake.
glossary.limit: Clock timing can work against sleep pressure; a person may feel tired yet remain awake.

glossary.limit: Arousal can be affected by a real environment as well as by worry.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
Feeling exhausted and being ready to sleep are related, but not identical. Sleep depends on more than how much effort a person has put in today.

Why can someone feel desperately tired and still struggle to fall asleep?
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

nodes.title: What sleep pressure means
nodes.body:
A drive for sleep that generally grows while we stay awake and reduces during sleep.

For example: After a long day awake, someone begins to feel increasingly sleepy.

One important limit: A nap can reduce some sleep pressure even if somebody still wants an early night.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: After a long day awake, someone begins to feel increasingly sleepy. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports sleep pressure. A drive for sleep that generally grows while we stay awake and reduces during sleep. A nap can reduce some sleep pressure even if somebody still wants an early night.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

options.feedback: This description follows from the example. A drive for sleep that generally grows while we stay awake and reduces during sleep.

options.label: This most directly illustrates Circadian timing.
options.feedback: Circadian timing is a genuine psychological idea, but the observation by itself does not establish it. Clock timing can work against sleep pressure; a person may feel tired yet remain awake.

options.label: This most directly illustrates Arousal.
options.feedback: Arousal is a genuine psychological idea, but the observation by itself does not establish it. Arousal can be affected by a real environment as well as by worry.

options.label: This most directly illustrates Consistency.
options.feedback: Consistency is a genuine psychological idea, but the observation by itself does not establish it. Consistency helps many people but must be adapted around work and individual health needs.

nodes.title: What circadian timing means
nodes.body:
Internal daily rhythms that influence when the body is prepared for sleep and wakefulness.

For example: A night-shift worker finds the morning alerting despite a long period awake.

One important limit: Clock timing can work against sleep pressure; a person may feel tired yet remain awake.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

nodes.title: What arousal means
nodes.body:
The body's and mind's level of activation, which can make settling into sleep harder.

For example: Someone becomes more alert each time they check the clock and worry about being awake.

One important limit: Arousal can be affected by a real environment as well as by worry.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

nodes.title: What consistency means
nodes.body:
Keeping a reasonably regular pattern that helps the body anticipate periods of sleep.

For example: A person wakes at a similar time on most days after a period of irregular shifts.

One important limit: Consistency helps many people but must be adapted around work and individual health needs.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Bea finished a night shift and feels exhausted at 10 am, but has been struggling to fall asleep when she gets home.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.
nodes.scenario: Bea finished a night shift and feels exhausted at 10 am, but has been struggling to fall asleep when she gets home.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I've been awake for sixteen hours. I should fall asleep immediately.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Do you usually find it easy to sleep when the sun is up?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: No. I feel worn out, but my brain seems unusually alert at this time.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What was your sleep schedule before night shifts?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
checks.counterexample: Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

items.label: “I've been awake for sixteen hours. I should fall asleep immediately.”
Time awake builds homeostatic sleep pressure, while circadian timing changes biological readiness for sleep. These processes can point in different directions after shift work.
“Do you usually find it easy to sleep when the sun is up?”
Caffeine, bright light, environment and stress may also affect Bea's alertness; a single sleep episode cannot identify one mechanism with certainty.

nodes.title: Why the distinction matters
nodes.body:
Caffeine, bright light, environment and stress may also affect Bea's alertness; a single sleep episode cannot identify one mechanism with certainty.

Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Time awake builds homeostatic sleep pressure, while circadian timing changes biological readiness for sleep. These processes can point in different directions after shift work.

Another possibility: Caffeine, bright light, environment and stress may also affect Bea's alertness; a single sleep episode cannot identify one mechanism with certainty.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Record habitual sleep times, shift schedule and light/caffeine exposure rather than judging only by tiredness. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Record habitual sleep times, shift schedule and light/caffeine exposure rather than judging only by tiredness.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: Bea sleeps more easily after several days on a consistent day-shift schedule, even when the total time awake is similar.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The difference supports a contribution from circadian timing, although work stress and light exposure also changed.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Ready for a real case
lessons.teach: You have the concepts. Now practise using them without jumping beyond the evidence.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

lessons.title: Why an early bedtime isn't enough
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of sleep pressure accumulated through waking.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), A Two Process Model of Sleep Regulation; NICE insomnia guidance.
nodes.scenario: Nora woke just after noon and is trying to sleep at nine in the evening.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I've been in bed an hour and I'm wide awake.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: When did you get up this morning?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: After twelve. I thought an early night would reset the schedule.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Are you sleepy, or mainly worried about tomorrow?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Mostly worried. I'm checking the clock because I need eight hours.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Going to bed early doesn't guarantee the body is ready for sleep.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Nora may be experiencing a separate persistent sleep disorder that needs assessment.
Nora may not have a sufficiently comfortable sleeping environment.
Nora may have relatively little sleep pressure at the chosen bedtime, compounded by sleep-related worry.
Caffeine used to manage the night shift may be delaying sleep once she returns home.
options.feedback: This would be relevant if intake and timing support it; neither has been recorded yet.

options.label: Caffeine, bright light, environment and stress may also affect Bea's alertness; a single sleep episode cannot identify one mechanism with certainty.
options.feedback: This is a plausible competing hypothesis. Its relative strength depends on whether it accounts for the most revealing details.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Nora may have relatively little sleep pressure at the chosen bedtime, compounded by sleep-related worry. Nora may be experiencing a separate persistent sleep disorder that needs assessment. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Insomnia has multiple causes, and persistent difficulty merits appropriate assessment. Sleep needs and health circumstances vary.

checks.prompt: You are Nora. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

lessons.title: Try it in another situation

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A traveller feels exhausted after flying overnight yet lies awake in their hotel at the destination's usual bedtime, which is midday according to their previous body clock.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Time awake builds homeostatic sleep pressure, while circadian timing changes biological readiness for sleep. These processes can point in different directions after shift work.

Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

glossary.definition: A drive for sleep that generally grows while we stay awake and reduces during sleep.
glossary.example: After a long day awake, someone begins to feel increasingly sleepy.
glossary.limit: A nap can reduce some sleep pressure even if somebody still wants an early night.

glossary.definition: Internal daily rhythms that influence when the body is prepared for sleep and wakefulness.
glossary.example: A night-shift worker finds the morning alerting despite a long period awake.
glossary.limit: Clock timing can work against sleep pressure; a person may feel tired yet remain awake.

glossary.definition: The body's and mind's level of activation, which can make settling into sleep harder.
glossary.example: Someone becomes more alert each time they check the clock and worry about being awake.
glossary.limit: Arousal can be affected by a real environment as well as by worry.

glossary.definition: Keeping a reasonably regular pattern that helps the body anticipate periods of sleep.
glossary.example: A person wakes at a similar time on most days after a period of irregular shifts.
glossary.limit: Consistency helps many people but must be adapted around work and individual health needs.
